claim: Expansion of biliary epithelial cells (BECs) during ductular reaction (DR) is observed in liver diseases including cystic fibrosis (CF).
source: Expansion of biliary epithelial cells (BECs) during ductular reaction (DR) is observed in liver diseases including cystic fibrosis (CF), and associated with inflammation and fibrosis, albeit without complete understanding of underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known observation in liver diseases.

claim: Ductular reaction is associated with inflammation and fibrosis.
source: Expansion of biliary epithelial cells (BECs) during ductular reaction (DR) is observed in liver diseases including cystic fibrosis (CF), and associated with inflammation and fibrosis, albeit without complete understanding of underlying mechanism.
evidence: This association is stated in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: KO2 mice show gradual liver repopulation with BEC-derived β-catenin-positive hepatocytes and resolution of injury.
source: KO2 show gradual liver repopulation with BEC-derived β-catenin-positive hepatocytes and resolution of injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: KO1 mice showed persistent loss of β-catenin after CDE diet injury.
source: KO1 showed persistent loss of β-catenin, NF-κB activation in BECs, progressive DR and fibrosis, reminiscent of CF histology.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry and gene expression data.

claim: KO1 mice showed NF-κB activation in BECs.
source: KO1 showed persistent loss of β-catenin, NF-κB activation in BECs, progressive DR and fibrosis, reminiscent of CF histology.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by confocal microscopy showing nuclear p65 translocation.

claim: KO1 mice showed progressive DR and fibrosis reminiscent of CF histology.
source: KO1 showed persistent loss of β-catenin, NF-κB activation in BECs, progressive DR and fibrosis, reminiscent of CF histology.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological analysis and comparison with CF patient samples.

claim: β-catenin, NF-κB, and CFTR interact in BECs.
source: We identify interactions of β-catenin, NFκB, and CF transmembranous conductance regulator (CFTR) in BECs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Loss of CFTR leads to NF-κB activation, DR, and inflammation.
source: Loss of CFTR or β-catenin led to NF-κB activation, DR, and inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CFTR knockdown experiments in cell culture.

claim: Loss of β-catenin leads to NF-κB activation, DR, and inflammation.
source: Loss of CFTR or β-catenin led to NF-κB activation, DR, and inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from KO1 mice.

claim: Disruption of the β-catenin-NF-κB-CFTR interactome may contribute to hepatic pathology of CF.
source: Thus, we report a novel β-catenin-NFκB-CFTR interactome in BECs, and its disruption may contribute to hepatic pathology of CF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison with CF patient samples.

claim: Cirrhosis is the 11th leading cause of death globally.
source: Currently, cirrhosis is the 11th leading cause of death globally, and the incidence of liver disease continues to rise as conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and alcoholic liver disease continue to prevail (Asrani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Asrani et al., 2019.

claim: The incidence of liver disease continues to rise as conditions such as NAFLD and alcoholic liver disease continue to prevail.
source: Currently, cirrhosis is the 11th leading cause of death globally, and the incidence of liver disease continues to rise as conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and alcoholic liver disease continue to prevail (Asrani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Asrani et al., 2019.

claim: Loss of hepatocyte differentiation in chronic liver diseases contributes to loss of key hepatic functions.
source: Loss of hepatocyte differentiation in chronic liver diseases and ESLD, either due to much needed hepithelial proliferation for repair, or as an adaptation to escape injury, seems to contribute to not only loss of key hepatic functions, but is also causally associated with increased immune response and hepatic fibrosis (Argemi, 2019; Nishikawa, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Argemi, 2019 and Nishikawa, 2015.

claim: Loss of hepatocyte differentiation in chronic liver diseases is causally associated with increased immune response and hepatic fibrosis.
source: Loss of hepatocyte differentiation in chronic liver diseases and ESLD, either due to much needed hepithelial proliferation for repair, or as an adaptation to escape injury, seems to contribute to not only loss of key hepatic functions, but is also causally associated with increased immune response and hepatic fibrosis (Argemi, 2019; Nishikawa, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Argemi, 2019 and Nishikawa, 2015.

claim: BECs undergo proliferation to replace dying BECs in cholangiopathies or cystic liver diseases.
source: As an important hepithelial cell type, BECs are known to undergo proliferation to replace dying BECs in cholangiopathies or cystic liver diseases, as well as can under phenotypic switch to generate de novo hepatocytes when hepatocytes are chronically injured and/or are unable to optimally proliferate, phenomena termed as ductular reaction (DR) (Sato et al., 2019; Wilson and Rudnick, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sato et al., 2019 and Wilson and Rudnick, 2019.

claim: BECs can undergo phenotypic switch to generate de novo hepatocytes when hepatocytes are chronically injured and/or are unable to optimally proliferate.
source: As an important hepithelial cell type, BECs are known to undergo proliferation to replace dying BECs in cholangiopathies or cystic liver diseases, as well as can under phenotypic switch to generate de novo hepatocytes when hepatocytes are chronically injured and/or are unable to optimally proliferate, phenomena termed as ductular reaction (DR) (Sato et al., 2019; Wilson and Rudnick, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sato et al., 2019 and Wilson and Rudnick, 2019.

claim: Reactive ductules can secrete pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines to induce inflammation, activate myofibroblasts, and induce fibrosis.
source: Reactive ductules, however, can secrete pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines to induce inflammation, activate myofibroblasts, and induce fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The extent of DR correlates with fibrosis in many types of liver injuries.
source: The extent of DR correlates with fibrosis in many types of liver injuries (Lowes et al., 1999; Richardson, 2007; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lowes et al., 1999; Richardson, 2007; and Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: YAP1 has been implicated in reactive DR.
source: The molecular underpinnings of reactive DR are incompletely understood although molecules like Yes-associated protein-1 (YAP1) have been implicated (Planas-Paz, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Planas-Paz, 2019.

claim: β-Catenin is a well-known mediator of hepatocyte proliferation.
source: β-Catenin, the major downstream effector of the Wnt signaling, is a well-known mediator of hepatocyte proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Liver-specific β-catenin knockout (KO1) mice show delayed liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy or after toxicant-induced liver injury.
source: Liver-specific (hepatocyte and BECs) β-catenin knockout (KO1) mice generated by breeding β-catenin-floxed and albumin-cre mice show delayed liver regeneration (LR) after partial hepatectomy or after toxicant-induced liver injury (Apte, 2009; Tan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Apte, 2009 and Tan et al., 2006.

claim: CDE diet triggered greater steatosis, cell death, DR, inflammation, and fibrosis in KO1 than wild-type (WT1).
source: When KO1 were administered choline-deficient, ethionine-supplemented (CDE) diet, it triggered greater steatosis, cell death, DR, inflammation, and fibrosis than wild-type (WT1), and upon switching to normal diet for 2 weeks for recovery, continued to show greater injury due to an impairment of hepatocyte proliferation (Akhurst, 2001; Russell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akhurst, 2001 and Russell, 2019.

claim: KO1 mice continued to show greater injury after switching to normal diet for 2 weeks due to an impairment of hepatocyte proliferation.
source: When KO1 were administered choline-deficient, ethionine-supplemented (CDE) diet, it triggered greater steatosis, cell death, DR, inflammation, and fibrosis than wild-type (WT1), and upon switching to normal diet for 2 weeks for recovery, continued to show greater injury due to an impairment of hepatocyte proliferation (Akhurst, 2001; Russell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akhurst, 2001 and Russell, 2019.

claim: CDE-fed hepatocyte-only β-catenin KO (KO2) showed greater injury, fibrosis, and DR similar to KO1.
source: Similar greater injury, fibrosis, and DR were observed in CDE-fed hepatocyte-only β-catenin KO (KO2), generated by delivering adeno-associated virus serotype 8 carrying a plasmid encoding Cre recombinase under a hepatocyte-specific thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) promoter (AAV8-TBG-Cre) into the β-catenin-floxed mice (Russell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Russell, 2019.

claim: Liver repair occurred through BEC-to-hepatocyte transdifferentiation in KO2 upon recovery for 2 weeks and up to 6 months on normal diet.
source: Intriguingly, labeling BECs for fate-tracing showed the liver repair to occur through BEC-to-hepatocyte transdifferentiation upon recovery for 2 weeks and up to 6 months on normal diet, although long-term impact on injury resolution, inflammation, DR, and fibrosis was not studied in either model (Russell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Russell, 2019.

claim: KO2 mice had elevated serum ALT and total bilirubin levels compared to WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet.
source: KO2 mice had elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and total bilirubin (BR) levels than WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet, but returned to normal at 2 weeks onwards after switching to normal diet, similar to WT2, although BR levels tended to be higher in KO2 up to 3 months of recovery (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Serum ALT and bilirubin levels in KO2 returned to normal at 2 weeks after switching to normal diet.
source: KO2 mice had elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and total bilirubin (BR) levels than WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet, but returned to normal at 2 weeks onwards after switching to normal diet, similar to WT2, although BR levels tended to be higher in KO2 up to 3 months of recovery (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Bilirubin levels tended to be higher in KO2 than WT2 up to 3 months of recovery.
source: KO2 mice had elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and total bilirubin (BR) levels than WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet, but returned to normal at 2 weeks onwards after switching to normal diet, similar to WT2, although BR levels tended to be higher in KO2 up to 3 months of recovery (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was increased in WT2 and KO2 after 2 weeks of CDE injury but returned to normal at 2 weeks of recovery in both groups.
source: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was increased in WT2 and KO2 after 2 weeks of CDE injury but returned to normal at 2 weeks of recovery in both groups (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: There were increased numbers of β-catenin-positive hepatocytes in KO2 at 3 months and 6 months of recovery.
source: Likewise, by immunohistochemistry (IHC) for β-catenin that is only present in BECs in KO2 at baseline, there were increased numbers of β-catenin-positive hepatocytes at 3 months and 6 months of recovery (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: β-catenin gene (Ctnnb1) expression showed increasing expression in KO2 livers over time, becoming comparable to WT2 at 6 months.
source: RT-PCR for β-catenin gene (Ctnnb1) expression showed increasing expression in KO2 livers over time, becoming comparable to WT2 at 6 months (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Zone 3 GS-positive cells are present in KO2 at 6-month recovery time point.
source: Since glutamine synthetase (GS) is a β-catenin-specific target, we also examined its protein by IHC in WT2 and KO2 at the 6-month recovery time. Indeed, like in WT2, zone 3 GS-positive cells are present in KO2 showing β-catenin presence and activation at this time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: KO2 showed greater collagen deposition than WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet and persisted at 2 weeks of recovery.
source: Sirius Red staining for fibrosis showed greater collagen deposition in KO2 than WT2 at 2 weeks of CDE diet and persisted at 2 weeks of recovery (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius Red staining data presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: KO2 continued to show fibrosis at 3 months despite being on normal diet and lack of any ongoing injury.
source: Interestingly, despite being on normal diet and lack of any ongoing injury, KO2 continued to show fibrosis at 3 months, eventually resolving at 6 months (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius Red staining data presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Fibrosis in KO2 resolved at 6 months of recovery.
source: Interestingly, despite being on normal diet and lack of any ongoing injury, KO2 continued to show fibrosis at 3 months, eventually resolving at 6 months (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius Red staining data presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Expression of Col1a1 and Tgfβ2 tended to be higher in KO2 compared to WT2 mice at 3-month recovery, but were comparable to WT2 at 6 months.
source: Likewise, expression of Col1a1 and Tgfβ2 tended to be higher in KO2 compared to WT2 mice at 3-month recovery, but were comparable to WT2 at 6 months (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: At 3 months of recovery, normal bile ducts are seen in WT2, whereas DR composed of flattened, non-luminal, and single or few cell clusters is evident throughout liver lobule in KO2.
source: At 3 months of recovery, normal bile ducts are seen in WT2, whereas DR composed of flattened, non-luminal, and single or few cell clusters is evident throughout liver lobule in KO2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by pan-cytokeratin staining data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: At 6 months of recovery, there was no DR in either WT2 or KO2.
source: At 6 months, there was no DR in either group (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by pan-cytokeratin staining data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Higher expression of Timp1 persisted in KO2 as compared to WT2 at all recovery times except 6 months.
source: Higher expression of Timp1 persisted in KO2 as compared to WT2 at all recovery times except 6 months, coinciding with resolution of fibrosis and DR (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Resolution of fibrosis and DR in KO2 coincided with normalization of Timp1 levels at 6 months.
source: Higher expression of Timp1 persisted in KO2 as compared to WT2 at all recovery times except 6 months, coinciding with resolution of fibrosis and DR (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between Timp1 levels and fibrosis/DR resolution.

claim: KO1 mice showed severe liver injury with significantly higher serum ALT and total bilirubin after 2 weeks of CDE diet compared to WT1.
source: We observed severe liver injury in KO1 mice, shown by significantly higher serum ALT and total BR after 2 weeks of CDE diet compared to WT1.
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Serum ALT levels in KO1 and WT1 mice decreased to normal levels during recovery.
source: During recovery, serum ALT levels in KO1 and WT1 mice decreased to normal levels (Figure 3B), while BR remained mildly elevated in KO1 mice up to 3 months of recovery as compared to WT1, which returned to normal at 2 weeks of recovery (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Bilirubin remained mildly elevated in KO1 mice up to 3 months of recovery as compared to WT1, which returned to normal at 2 weeks of recovery.
source: During recovery, serum ALT levels in KO1 and WT1 mice decreased to normal levels (Figure 3B), while BR remained mildly elevated in KO1 mice up to 3 months of recovery as compared to WT1, which returned to normal at 2 weeks of recovery (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Serum ALP levels were comparably increased in WT1 and KO1 at 2 weeks of CDE injury and returned to normal levels at 2-week recovery.
source: Serum ALP levels were comparably increased in WT1 and KO1 at 2 weeks of CDE injury and returned to normal levels at 2-week recovery (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by serum biochemistry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: IHC for β-catenin and RT-PCR for Ctnnb1 showed continued absence in KO1 and not WT1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery on normal diet.
source: Since β-catenin is lacking in hepithelial cells in the KO1 livers, IHC for β-catenin and RT-PCR for Ctnnb1 showed continued absence in KO1 and not WT1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery on normal diet (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and RT-PCR data presented in Figure 3C, D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a complete absence of GS in zone 3 hepatocytes in KO1 at 6-month recovery time point.
source: As a surrogate for β-catenin presence and activity, we also assessed GS by IHC in WT1 and KO1 at the 6-month recovery time. Unlike WT1, there is a complete absence of GS in zone 3 hepatocytes in KO1 showing continued absence of β-catenin at this time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: KO1 showed continued fibrosis especially in the periportal area at 3 months and 6 months despite normalization of serum transaminases during recovery.
source: Despite normalization of serum transaminases during recovery, we observed continued fibrosis especially in the periportal area in KO1 and especially at 3 months and 6 months by Sirius Red staining, whereas WT1 mice displayed resolution of fibrosis as early as 2-week recovery (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius Red staining data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: WT1 mice displayed resolution of fibrosis as early as 2-week recovery.
source: Despite normalization of serum transaminases during recovery, we observed continued fibrosis especially in the periportal area in KO1 and especially at 3 months and 6 months by Sirius Red staining, whereas WT1 mice displayed resolution of fibrosis as early as 2-week recovery (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius Red staining data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of Col1a1 tended to be higher in KO1 mice during recovery.
source: Additionally, expression of Col1a1 tended to be higher in KO1 mice during recovery (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The DR in KO1 changed from flattened, invasive, and without lumen morphology from early time points to numerous small luminal structures lined by a single layer of PanCK-positive columnar cells at 3 months and 6 months.
source: Furthermore, the DR was peculiar and composed of numerous small luminal structures lined by a single layer of PanCK-positive columnar cells at 3 months and 6 months, rather than more flattened and invasive DR without lumen seen at earlier stages of CDE injury and recovery in both WT1, KO1, and even KO2 (Figures 4D and 2D).
evidence: This is supported by pan-cytokeratin staining data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Enhanced gene expression for Krt19 and Epcam was evident in KO1 at 3 months and 6 months of recovery.
source: Enhanced gene expression for Krt19 and Epcam was simultaneously evident in KO1 at these times (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Significantly more BECs were proliferating in KO1 compared to WT1 mice at 3-month recovery.
source: To determine if the continued DR was due to ongoing BEC proliferation, we co-stained KO1 livers from 3-month recovery with PanCK and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Significantly more BECs were proliferating in KO1 compared to WT1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: A subset of BECs in DR were positive for phospho-Erk1/2 (p-Erk1/2) in KO1.
source: A subset of BECs in DR were also positive for phospho-Erk1/2 (p-Erk1/2), known for regulating BEC proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Pepe-Mooney, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and a citation to Pepe-Mooney, 2019.

claim: Timp1 tended to be upregulated in KO1 mice at all times but significantly at 6-month recovery time.
source: Timp1 tended to be upregulated in KO1 mice at all times but significantly at 6-month recovery time (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: CDE diet-fed KO2 or WT2 mice showed no significant increase in hepatic bile acids at any time.
source: However, CDE diet-fed KO2 or WT2 mice showed no significant increase in hepatic bile acids at any time, suggesting these to not be driving DR or fibrosis in this model (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by bile acid measurement data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: No significant hepatocyte senescence was observed by p21 IHC in WT2 or KO2 mice during long-term recovery from CDE diet.
source: We also investigated cell senescence as a possible driver of DR and fibrosis (Wei-Yu et al., 2015). However, no significant hepatocyte senescence was observed by p21 IHC in WT2 or KO2 mice during long-term recovery from CDE diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cleaved caspase 3 staining showed minimal cell death in both WT1 and KO1 mice at 3 months of recovery.
source: Cleaved caspase 3 staining showed minimal cell death in both WT1 and KO1 mice at 3 months of recovery (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: At 6 months of recovery, immunoprecipitation with E-cadherin showed an association of E-cadherin to β-catenin in KO2 and with γ-catenin in KO1.
source: However, at 6 months of recovery, immunoprecipitation (IP) with E-cadherin showed an association of E-cadherin to β-catenin in KO2 and with γ-catenin in KO1, as has been shown in β-catenin-deficient livers by us previously (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D; Pradhan-Sundd, 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and a citation to Pradhan-Sundd, 2018b.

claim: Mice lacking Th1 immune signaling or interferon-γ showed impaired DR and decreased fibrosis after CDE diet.
source: Previously, the presence of immune cell infiltration has been shown to be essential in the development of DR and fibrosis. Mice lacking Th1 immune signaling or interferon-γ showed impaired DR and decreased fibrosis after CDE diet (Knight, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Knight, 2007.

claim: CD45-positive cells were present in high numbers in WT2 and KO2 mice after 2-week CDE diet, which declined in WT2 after 2 weeks of recovery.
source: There were high numbers of CD45-positive cells in WT2 and KO2 mice after 2-week CDE diet, which declined in WT2 after 2 weeks of recovery, decreased overall but persisted pan-lobularly in KO2 up to 3 months, and normalized to WT2 levels by 6 months (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: CD45-positive cells decreased overall but persisted pan-lobularly in KO2 up to 3 months, and normalized to WT2 levels by 6 months.
source: There were high numbers of CD45-positive cells in WT2 and KO2 mice after 2-week CDE diet, which declined in WT2 after 2 weeks of recovery, decreased overall but persisted pan-lobularly in KO2 up to 3 months, and normalized to WT2 levels by 6 months (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: CD45-positive cells were present in high numbers in both WT1 and KO1 at 2 weeks of CDE diet, and while these numbers gradually returned to baseline in WT2 at 2 weeks of recovery, a more intense periportal-appearing infiltration was seen in KO1 especially at 3 months and 6 months.
source: CD45-positive cells were present in high numbers in both WT1 and KO1 at 2 weeks of CDE diet, and while these numbers gradually returned to baseline in WT2 at 2 weeks of recovery, a more intense periportal-appearing infiltration was seen in KO1 especially at 3 months and 6 months (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: CD45-positive cell infiltration significantly resolved at 3 months and 6 months of recovery from CDE diet in both WT2 and KO2.
source: Quantification of the area occupied by CD45-positive cells at all time points revealed that CD45-positive cell infiltration significantly resolved at 3 months and 6 months of recovery from CDE diet in both WT2 and KO2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD45-positive cells in KO1 always tended to be higher than WT1 at all respective time points analyzed.
source: However, CD45-positive cells in KO1 always tended to be higher than WT1 at all respective time points analyzed.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Statistically significant and higher inflammation was observed in KO1 at 6 months as compared to WT1 at all time points.
source: Statistically significant and higher inflammation was observed in KO1 at 6 months as compared to WT1 at all time points (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In KO2 mice, BECs, αSMA-positive cells, and leukocytes were seen in close proximity to each other up to 3 months of recovery and returned to WT2 state at 6 months.
source: In KO2 mice, BECs, αSMA-positive cells, and leukocytes were seen in close proximity to each other up to 3 months of recovery and returned to WT2 state at 6 months (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by triple immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: KO1 livers showed closely associated CD45- and PanCK-positive cells at all times in contrast to WT1, which lacked CD45 cells at all times after 2 weeks of recovery.
source: KO1 livers showed closely associated CD45- and PanCK-positive cells at all times in contrast to WT1, which lacked CD45 cells at all times after 2 weeks of recovery (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by triple immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In KO1, αSMA-positive cells were not observed at any time after 2 weeks of recovery.
source: Intriguingly, even in KO1, αSMA-positive cells were not observed at any time after 2 weeks of recovery.
evidence: This is supported by triple immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Expression of Adgre1 (gene encoding macrophage marker F4/80) showed significant increase in KO1 compared to WT1 mice at 3-month recovery.
source: Analysis in whole livers for expression of Adgre1, gene encoding macrophage marker F4/80, showed significant increase in KO1 compared to WT1 mice at 3-month recovery (Figure 5D), and these macrophages were located close to the DR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 5D and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Macrophages in KO1 were located close to the DR.
source: Analysis in whole livers for expression of Adgre1, gene encoding macrophage marker F4/80, showed significant increase in KO1 compared to WT1 mice at 3-month recovery (Figure 5D), and these macrophages were located close to the DR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Itgam expression was significantly higher in KO1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery times.
source: Itgam expression was significantly higher in KO1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery times (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: There was increased staining for Ly6G in KO1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery times.
source: There was also increased staining for Ly6G, a marker for monocytes, granulocytes, and neutrophils, in KO1 at 3-month and 6-month recovery times (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: β-catenin has an inhibitory interaction with p65 subunit of NF-κB in hepatocytes.
source: We have previously shown an inhibitory interaction of β-catenin with p65 subunit of NF-κB in hepatocytes and the absence of β-catenin in KO1 led to increased NF-κB activation in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or tumor necrosis factor-α challenge (Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013.

claim: The absence of β-catenin in KO1 led to increased NF-κB activation in response to LPS or TNF-α challenge.
source: We have previously shown an inhibitory interaction of β-catenin with p65 subunit of NF-κB in hepatocytes and the absence of β-catenin in KO1 led to increased NF-κB activation in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or tumor necrosis factor-α challenge (Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013.

claim: Reactive ductules are a well-known source of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic cytokines.
source: Further, while immune cells are essential for DR and fibrosis, reactive ductules are a well-known source of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic cytokines and thus this cross-cellular signaling perpetuates overall injury (Fava et al., 2005; Pinto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fava et al., 2005 and Pinto et al., 2018.

claim: At baseline in KO2, p65 subunit of NF-κB was present in the cytosol of the CK19-positive cells, as was β-catenin.
source: At baseline in KO2, p65 subunit of NF-κB was present in the cytosol of the CK19-positive cells, as was β-catenin (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: In KO1, at baseline, CK19-positive BECs lacked β-catenin and p65 was still evident in cytosol.
source: In KO1, at baseline, CK19-positive BECs lacked β-catenin and p65 was still evident in cytosol (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: At 2 weeks of CDE diet, a subset of CK19-positive BECs showed comparable nuclear p65 by confocal microscopy in both KO2 and KO1.
source: At 2 weeks of CDE diet, when DR and inflammation is ongoing in both KO2 and KO1 livers, a subset of CK19-positive BECs showed comparable nuclear p65 by confocal microscopy in both groups (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: At 6 months in KO2, β-catenin-positive, CK19-positive BECs showed only cytosolic p65 similar to baseline.
source: At 6 months in KO2, β-catenin-positive, CK19-positive BECs showed only cytosolic p65 similar to baseline (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: KO1 livers at 6-month recovery from CDE injury showed profound nuclear translocation of p65 in almost all CK19-positive BECs, which continued to lack β-catenin.
source: However, unlike at baseline, KO1 livers at 6-month recovery from CDE injury showed profound nuclear translocation of p65 in almost all CK19-positive BECs, which continued to lack β-catenin (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Relative to WT1, 44% of NF-κB downstream target genes (37/84) were upregulated in KO1, whereas 92% of genes (77/84) in KO2 livers were unchanged at 6 months of recovery.
source: Relative to WT1, we found a striking upregulation in the expression of 44% of genes (37/84) in KO1, whereas 92% of genes (77/84) in KO2 livers were unchanged at 6 months of recovery (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR array data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Clustergram showed KO2s were indistinguishable from WT1, but KO1 clearly separated from both groups.
source: Clustergram showed KO2s were indistinguishable from WT1, but KO1 clearly separated from both groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by clustergram data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of β-catenin in SMCCs induced p65 luciferase activity, which was three times greater than caused by 100 ng/ml LPS stimulation.
source: Knockdown of β-catenin in SMCCs, shown by a significant decrease in TOPFlash activity, induced p65 luciferase activity, which was three times greater than caused by 100 ng/ml LPS stimulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Expression of stable S45Y-β-catenin in SMCCs led to increased TOPFlash activity but significantly decreased p65 reporter activity with or without LPS.
source: Conversely, expression of stable S45Y-β-catenin or T41A-β-catenin (not shown) in SMCCs led to increased TOPFlash activity but significantly decreased p65 reporter activity with or without LPS (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Similar negative regulation of p65 by β-catenin was observed in MzChA and HuCCT1, two independent human CCA cell lines.
source: Similar negative regulation was also observed in MzChA and HuCCT1, two independent human CCA cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Upon β-catenin silencing, significantly higher levels of p65 were found in the nuclear compartment versus the controls, both without LPS, but more so following LPS treatment.
source: By WB, at baseline, notably higher levels of both p65 and β-catenin were evident in the cytoplasmic and not nuclear fraction. Upon β-catenin silencing, significantly higher levels of p65 were found in the nuclear compartment versus the controls, both without LPS, but more so following LPS treatment (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 7C and D.

claim: β-catenin-silenced SMCCs showed 75 upregulated and 122 downregulated genes.
source: Using a cutoff p-value ≤ 0.05 and abs(log2FC) ≥ 1.5, we found 335 β-catenin-regulated genes in BECs. Specifically, β-catenin-silenced SMCCs showed 75 upregulated and 122 downregulated, and β-catenin-active SMCCs showed 76 upregulated and 69 downregulated genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: β-catenin-active SMCCs showed 76 upregulated and 69 downregulated genes.
source: Using a cutoff p-value ≤ 0.05 and abs(log2FC) ≥ 1.5, we found 335 β-catenin-regulated genes in BECs. Specifically, β-catenin-silenced SMCCs showed 75 upregulated and 122 downregulated, and β-catenin-active SMCCs showed 76 upregulated and 69 downregulated genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: RELA (p65) was identified among the top transcription factors, with 9.6% of differentially expressed genes showing known RELA regulation (32/335, p=0.015).
source: RELA (p65) was identified among the top TFs (ranking by p-value), with 9.6% of DEGs showing known RELA regulation (32/335, p=0.015) and 15.2% (51/335, p=0.088) showing NF-κB binding sites (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by JASPAR analysis data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: 15.2% (51/335) of differentially expressed genes showed NF-κB binding sites (p=0.088).
source: RELA (p65) was identified among the top TFs (ranking by p-value), with 9.6% of DEGs showing known RELA regulation (32/335, p=0.015) and 15.2% (51/335, p=0.088) showing NF-κB binding sites (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by JASPAR analysis data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: β-catenin-silenced SMCCs showed modest but significant increase in CCL2, and a more pronounced and significant increase in CXCL5 expression.
source: Interestingly, from RNA-seq and by qPCR, we found modest but significant increase in CCL2, and a more pronounced and significant increase in CXCL5 expression, in the β-catenin-silenced SMCCs (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: After 6-month recovery from CDE diet, a significant induction in CCL2 and CXCL5 expression was noted in KO1 but not in WT1 and KO2.
source: After 6-month recovery from CDE diet, a significant induction in CCL2 and CXCL5 expression was noted in KO1 but not in WT1 and KO2 (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 7G.

claim: Robust β-catenin association with p65 was identified in SMCCs.
source: We identified robust β-catenin association with p65 in SMCCs (Figure 7H1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 7H.

claim: A fainter but positive β-catenin-p65 association was evident in whole livers.
source: A fainter but positive β-catenin-p65 association was evident in whole livers, likely due to low BEC representation in protein lysates from whole livers (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 7I.

claim: In WT1 liver at baseline, a notable colocalization of p65 and β-catenin was evident in the cytoplasm of BECs, which was expectedly absent in KO1.
source: In WT1 liver at baseline, a notable colocalization of p65 and β-catenin was evident in the cytoplasm of BECs, which was expectedly absent in KO1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: About 35% of p65 is associated with β-catenin in WT1, which was significantly greater than KO1.
source: Quantification of colocalization using ImageJ showed that about 35% of p65 is associated with β-catenin, which was significantly greater than KO1 (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data presented in Figure 7J.

claim: DR in CF was more homogeneous and appeared uniformly reminiscent of what was observed in 3-month and 6-month recovery times in KO1.
source: DR in CF was more homogeneous and appeared uniformly reminiscent of what we observed in 3-month and 6-month recovery times in KO1 (Figures 4D and 8A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 8A and comparison with Figure 4D.

claim: Strongest and significant nuclear p65 was consistently observed in DR seen in CF cases followed by PLD with only a very small subset of cells in DR showing nuclear p65 in AH.
source: Intriguingly, strongest and significant nuclear p65 was consistently observed in DR seen in CF cases followed by PLD with only a very small subset of cells in DR showing nuclear p65 in AH (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data presented in Figure 8B.

claim: A decrease in total β-catenin was observed in a single CF case from whom two independent frozen liver samples were available.
source: While β-catenin seem to be unaltered by IF staining in all three pathologies (Figure 8A), we observed a decrease in total β-catenin in a single CF case from whom two independent frozen liver samples were available (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 8C.

claim: CFTR (C-band and B-band) and p65 were pulled down with β-catenin in SMCCs.
source: We observed concomitant pulldown of both B-band (faster migrating core glycosylated immature form) as well as slowly migrating C-band (complex glycosylated form) (Chang, 2008), along with p65, when we immunoprecipitated β-catenin in SMCCs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: The expression of NF-κB target chemokines Ccl2 and Cxcl5 was significantly induced upon Cftr knockdown.
source: Likewise, the expression of NF-κB target chemokines Ccl2 and Cxcl5 was significantly induced upon Cftr knockdown (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 8F.

claim: Stabilization of β-catenin significantly decreased CFTR knockdown-induced p65 activation.
source: To query impact of β-catenin modulation, we next coexpressed stable-β-catenin (S45Y-mutant) in control and Cftr-siRNA-transfected SMCCs. Stabilization of β-catenin significantly decreased CFTR knockdown-induced p65 activation (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data presented in Figure 8E.

claim: No differences in the levels of total CFTR protein were observed between KO1 and WT1 at baseline and at 6 months of recovery from CDE diet.
source: To query if β-catenin loss in BECs had any impact on CFTR levels, we examined total levels of CFTR in KO1 and WT1 at baseline and at 6 months of recovery from CDE diet. We did not observe any differences in the levels of total CFTR protein, suggesting that CFTR may be an upstream effector of β-catenin while β-catenin does not regulate CFTR levels in BECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: CFTR may be an upstream effector of β-catenin while β-catenin does not regulate CFTR levels in BECs.
source: We did not observe any differences in the levels of total CFTR protein, suggesting that CFTR may be an upstream effector of β-catenin while β-catenin does not regulate CFTR levels in BECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that β-catenin loss does not affect CFTR levels.

claim: The role of DR as a source of de novo hepatocytes through the process of transdifferentiation is indisputable in preclinical models shown by many fate-tracing studies.
source: Its role as a source of de novo hepatocytes through the process of transdifferentiation is indisputable in preclinical models shown by many fate-tracing studies (Russell, 2019; Wei-Yu et al., 2015; Nejak-Bowen, 2020; Raven, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Russell, 2019; Wei-Yu et al., 2015; Nejak-Bowen, 2020; and Raven, 2017.

claim: DR can induce fibrosis by secreting pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic factors to contribute to the disease process.
source: At the same time, DR can induce fibrosis by secreting pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic factors to contribute to the disease process (Lowes et al., 1999; Richardson, 2007; Zhao et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2015a; Aguilar-Bravo, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lowes et al., 1999; Richardson, 2007; Zhao et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2015a; and Aguilar-Bravo, 2019.

claim: β-catenin-p65 complex exists in hepatocytes, breast and colon cancer cells, which could inhibit NF-κB activation.
source: Previously, we and others have described β-catenin-p65 complex in hepatocytes, breast and colon cancer cells, which could inhibit NF-κB activation (Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013; Deng, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nejak-Bowen et al., 2013 and Deng, 2002.

claim: β-catenin activation is observed in BECs within the DR during chronic liver injuries.
source: β-Catenin activation is observed in BECs within the DR during chronic liver injuries (Apte et al., 2008; Hu, 2007; Okabe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Apte et al., 2008; Hu, 2007; and Okabe, 2016.

claim: Unlike in hepatocytes, β-catenin activation in BECs does not play a role in their proliferation.
source: However, unlike in hepatocytes, β-catenin activation in BECs does not play a role in their proliferation (Russell, 2019; Okabe, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Russell, 2019 and Okabe, 2016.

claim: NF-κB activation has been shown to be important in BEC proliferation and DR by regulating Jagged/Notch signaling.
source: NF-κB activation has been shown to be important in BEC proliferation and DR by regulating Jagged/Notch signaling (Kim et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2015a.

claim: NF-κB in BECs has been suggested to play a role in inducing pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic milieu through regulating expression of many of its target genes including Ccl2 and Cxcl5.
source: And NF-κB in BECs has been suggested to play a role in inducing pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrogenic milieu as well through regulating expression of many of its target genes including Ccl2 and Cxcl5 (O'Hara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to O'Hara et al., 2013.

claim: Portal fibroblasts, macrophages, hepatocytes, and BECs have all been shown to secrete ligands like Wnt7a, Wnt7b, Wnt10a, and Wnt5a.
source: Molecular underpinnings of β-catenin stabilization in BECs especially during cholestatic liver injuries remain under investigation, although portal fibroblasts, macrophages, hepatocytes, and BECs have all been shown to secrete ligands like Wnt7a, Wnt7b, Wnt10a, and Wnt5a (Hu, 2007; Okabe, 2016; Wilson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu, 2007; Okabe, 2016; and Wilson, 2020.

claim: In human lung epithelial cells, a proteomic screen identified interaction of β-catenin with WT CFTR but not with ∆F508 CFTR.
source: Interestingly, in human lung epithelial cells, a proteomic screen identified interaction of β-catenin with WT CFTR but not with ∆F508 CFTR, a major site of LOF mutation in the CFTR (Pankow, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pankow, 2015.

claim: In mouse intestine, CFTR was shown to stabilize β-catenin and prevent its degradation.
source: Additionally, in mouse intestine, CFTR was shown to stabilize β-catenin and prevent its degradation (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: ∆F508 CFTR is unable to interact with β-catenin, leading to β-catenin degradation and eventually resulting in activation of NF-κB-mediated inflammatory cascade.
source: The same study showed that ∆F508 CFTR is unable to interact with β-catenin, leading to β-catenin degradation and eventually resulting in activation of NF-κB-mediated inflammatory cascade.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016 (implied from 'The same study').

claim: The classical pathology of liver disease in CF includes periductal inflammation, DR, periportal fibrosis, and focal biliary cirrhosis.
source: We believe that the classical pathology of liver disease in CF including periductal inflammation, DR, periportal fibrosis, and focal biliary cirrhosis may be explained by our observations, in addition to previously described mechanisms such as Rous sarcoma oncogene cellular homolog (Src)-dependent Toll-like receptor-4 activation (Fiorotto, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CF liver disease pathology.

claim: Src-dependent Toll-like receptor-4 activation has been previously described as a mechanism in CF liver disease.
source: We believe that the classical pathology of liver disease in CF including periductal inflammation, DR, periportal fibrosis, and focal biliary cirrhosis may be explained by our observations, in addition to previously described mechanisms such as Rous sarcoma oncogene cellular homolog (Src)-dependent Toll-like receptor-4 activation (Fiorotto, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fiorotto, 2016.

claim: Levels of Timp1 correlate with fibrosis.
source: Levels of Timp1 correlate with fibrosis, and several groups have investigated the use of TIMP1 levels as a biomarker for fibrosis in hepatitis C patients (Leroy, 2004; Boeker et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leroy, 2004 and Boeker et al., 2002.

claim: Mice with overexpression of TIMP1 developed dramatically more fibrosis after CCl4 treatment.
source: Mice with overexpression of TIMP1 developed dramatically more fibrosis after CCl4 treatment (Yoshiji, 2000), and TIMP1 transgenic mice showed impaired fibrosis resolution after cessation of CCl4 (Yoshiji, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshiji, 2000.

claim: TIMP1 transgenic mice showed impaired fibrosis resolution after cessation of CCl4.
source: Mice with overexpression of TIMP1 developed dramatically more fibrosis after CCl4 treatment (Yoshiji, 2000), and TIMP1 transgenic mice showed impaired fibrosis resolution after cessation of CCl4 (Yoshiji, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshiji, 2002.
